{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"Imagine opening a courthouse door and finding a tollbooth where the handle should be. You can see that a case exists, but your access to the record sits inside a private database, priced for firms that can charge the cost back to someone else. I think that arrangement gets the basic nature of a public record wrong. A court document belongs to the public because public power made it consequential, because a subscription company has made it searchable.

A public record is a civic necessity. It is part of the machinery by which we watch judges, prosecutors, police, landlords, employers, and one another when power gets used against somebody. If you’re trying to understand why your neighbor lost a home, how a prosecutor handled a charge, or whether a judge follows a stated rule, you need the filing, order, and docket (and sometimes the only way to check a claim). You can’t evaluate public power from a press release. That’s like judging a game from the scoreboard while the referee keeps the rules in a locked drawer.

The private database may make a difficult task easier. Fine. Search, bulk downloads, alerts, and clean interfaces take work – and somebody has to do that work. But convenience isn’t ownership. When a company puts a meter in front of a public record, it turns a civic right into a market at the exact point where the public needs scrutiny. We’re told, implicitly, that you may look, provided your institution can afford the looking. That isn’t access; it’s permission with an invoice attached.

This matters most when the person searching has the least money and the most need. A tenant facing eviction, a defendant without counsel, a local reporter, a student, or a small nonprofit can’t treat a monthly bill as pocket change. You’re asked to investigate the institution that governs your life, then handed a shopping cart. The missing document can determine whether you understand a deadline, spot a pattern, or find the earlier ruling that changes the meaning of the later one. That’s a choke point.

We should fund direct access as civic infrastructure – the way we fund the courthouse itself. Give people readable court websites, searchable dockets, downloadable documents, stable links, and archives that don’t vanish when a contract changes. I’m not arguing that every document must shed every safeguard. Sealed material, personal identifiers, and legitimate security limits still require judgment (including sealed material and personal identifiers). But the exception can’t swallow the rule, and privacy can’t become a magic word that excuses a closed system.

What happens when the official portal is clumsy or incomplete? You’ll hear the familiar answer: the private service adds value. Sometimes it does (and sometimes it does). Yet the public agency still has to publish the record in a usable form, because a private layer can’t be the only bridge between a person and the law. If you’re relying on an intermediary, you’re relying on its prices, retention choices, errors, and idea of what deserves to be easy. We’ve seen this pattern elsewhere: a public function becomes a platform, the platform becomes a gate, and the gate starts collecting rent.

I’ve spent enough time reading arguments about technology to distrust the word “friction” when it means exclusion. The friction here isn’t neutral. It falls on the reader who can’t expense a subscription and on the group that can’t hire a researcher. Meanwhile, the organization with money gets speed, context, and a searchable memory of government action. That’s a hell of a way to run a democracy (without special permission).

So here is the demand. Make digital court records available directly, without an expensive private database standing between the public and the public’s own courts. You should be able to search a docket, read an order, download a filing, and share it without asking a vendor’s permission. We can pay for reliable systems, publish clear standards, and build privacy protections into the design. We can also let private companies compete on better tools, as long as competition improves the public commons instead of replacing it.

I don’t want a court system that is formally open and practically opaque. I want you to be able to inspect the machinery that can fine you, evict you, confine you, or take your children. We’re all safer when the record is reachable before a crisis, rather than only after someone with money has assembled it. A public court record should be a window into public power – a curtain with a monthly fee.","omitted":[{"habit":"opponents-allies-sources / o12","why":"No verified source, quotation, named opponent position, or linked evidence was supplied for this topic."}],"refused":""}
